seacell.origin: SeaCell is a lyocell fiber into which ground seaweed is incorporated, so its generic fiber is lyocell and most of its mass is wood-pulp cellulose. Published accounts from 2006 describe it as developed on the lyocell process of Zimmer AG, a German engineering company in Frankfurt, and a clinical study of the silver-activated variant, SeaCell Active, credits SeaCell GmbH of Rudolstadt, Germany. The brand's current official page is hosted by smartfiber. Seaweed species, loading levels and present-day production partners could not be verified from public sources, so buyers should request them.
seacell.structure: The matrix is lyocell: cellulose II, highly oriented and crystalline, with a smooth, round cross-section. Seaweed material is dispersed within the fiber rather than chemically bonded to the cellulose. Researchers at Jena described a particular property of the SeaCell fiber as its capacity to bind and absorb substances; in SeaCell Active, silver is taken up by the fully formed cellulose fiber through metal sorption during an activation step. How much seaweed remains accessible at the surface after washing, and what it contributes chemically, is not quantified in public data.
seacell.process: As Zimmer AG described it, cellulose is dissolved in the lyocell system of cellulose, water and N-methylmorpholine N-oxide, a process able to handle diverse pulp types after suitable pretreatment. Seaweed is incorporated during fiber production, and filaments are formed by the dry-jet wet lyocell route, washed and finished. For SeaCell Active, a further activation step charges the fiber with metal ions, silver in the published studies, to make it antibacterial. The developer stated that neither the seaweed nor the activation impaired lyocell's textile properties. Plant-specific solvent recovery and seaweed content should come from current producer data.
seacell.performance: In use SeaCell behaves as lyocell: absorbent, strong when wet compared with viscose, prone to wet fibrillation and charring rather than melting. Evidence for added function concerns the silver-activated form. Laboratory studies showed dose-dependent activity of SeaCell Active against Candida species, Staphylococcus aureus and Escherichia coli, and a randomized, single-blinded study in 37 people with atopic dermatitis found less S. aureus colonization with silver-loaded seaweed-fiber T-shirts than with cotton over eight weeks. Claims that plain seaweed content benefits skin rest on producer statements rather than such trials.
seacell.identify: Burn tests are indicative only and show cellulose behavior: rapid burning, a paper-like smell and soft ash. Microscopy may show dispersed particles in otherwise smooth, round lyocell fibers, and elemental analysis can detect silver in the Active grade, but no standard test identifies the brand. In safety testing, no silver release from the fibers was detected, and none was found in the skin's outer layer or in serum. Retail phrases such as 'seaweed fabric' overstate the seaweed share, since the fiber is mainly cellulose from wood.
seacell.labeling: SeaCell is a trademark, not a generic fiber name. In the United States the fiber is labeled lyocell (or rayon) under the Textile Fiber Products Identification Act and 16 CFR 303.7, and in the EU it is lyocell under Regulation (EU) No 1007/2011; additives do not create a new generic name. Antibacterial or skin-benefit statements are separate claims needing substantiation for the specific product, and silver-treated textiles may fall under additional chemical or biocide rules depending on jurisdiction. Any certification should be checked on the certificate for the specific yarn or fabric.
seacell.past: SeaCell appears in the scientific literature by 2006, when solvent-spun cellulose had made it practical to add functional particles to the spinning dope without viscose chemistry. That year a Zimmer AG author described the seaweed fiber and its silver-activated version, and dermatologists at Friedrich Schiller University Jena published in vitro antifungal and antibacterial tests, followed by a patch test in 111 volunteers showing no sensitization and a 2010 trial in atopic dermatitis. The brand is now presented on smartfiber's website. Launch dates, ownership transfers and current production volumes could not be verified from primary sources.
facts: silver loaded by metal sorption (SeaCell Active)
37 atopic dermatitis patients, 8 weeks, less S. aureus colonization than with cotton
limited; seaweed share and species not published

coolmax.origin: COOLMAX is a moisture-management brand whose core product is polyester (PET) fiber with a profiled, non-round cross-section. A 2013 sports-science study attributed the fiber to INVISTA of Wichita, Kansas; the brand's own website now presents it within The LYCRA Company's portfolio, and readers should confirm current ownership, since that company went through a Chapter 11 restructuring in 2026. The name covers fibers, yarns and fabric specifications used by mills under the program, including blended and recycled-content variants, rather than one single fiber.
coolmax.structure: The polymer is ordinary PET: hydrophobic, thermoplastic and low in moisture uptake. What distinguishes the fiber is geometry. The 2013 study describes it as a 100% profiled cross-section polyester fiber, and textile researchers choose COOLMAX yarns specifically for enhanced wicking, the capillary flow of liquid along channels between and within the filaments. Research fabrics have paired it as a sheath around lyocell cores, with polypropylene in weft knits and with cotton in plated and 3D woven structures. Exact profiles vary by grade and are not independently documented here.
coolmax.process: In general practice for profiled fibers, PET chip, virgin or recycled, is melt spun through shaped spinneret holes, quenched, drawn and often textured while preserving the channels; grade-specific details are the producer's. Mills then knit or weave the yarn, frequently with elastane, cotton or other fibers, and may add hydrophilic finishes. Researchers have built COOLMAX yarn into two-sided knits, into 3D woven fabrics with a hydrophilic gradient, and into woven and stitched microfluidic channels for wearable sweat sensors, all relying on its capillary wicking. Fabric construction matters as much as fiber shape.
coolmax.performance: Polyester absorbs almost no water, so COOLMAX fabrics manage sweat by wicking it through and along the fabric for evaporation rather than holding it. In a sweating-manikin study of one-layer tight-fitting sportswear, a thin COOLMAX fabric maintained evaporative cooling efficiency well, while a thicker merino fabric performed worst, and fabric thickness strongly affected results. Wearers perceive fabrics with good liquid moisture management as less wet under heavy sweating. Stretching knitted cotton-COOLMAX fabrics opens pores and lowers ultraviolet protection. Like other polyester, it keeps its strength wet, dries quickly and melts under high heat.
coolmax.identify: Burn tests are indicative only: like other polyester, the fiber melts, shrinks from the flame and leaves a hard bead. Cross-sectional microscopy can reveal non-round, channeled profiles, which support but do not prove the brand, since many unbranded wicking polyesters use similar shapes. FTIR identifies PET. No laboratory test confirms the COOLMAX name; brand identity depends on hangtags and program documentation.
coolmax.labeling: COOLMAX is a trademark, not a generic fiber name. US labels must name polyester, plus any spandex or other fibers, under the Textile Fiber Products Identification Act and 16 CFR 303.7, and EU labels use polyester under Regulation (EU) No 1007/2011. Recycled-content variants need substantiated recycled claims, commonly supported by chain-of-custody certification such as the Global Recycled Standard, and cooling or wicking statements are performance claims tied to particular test methods and fabrics.
coolmax.past: COOLMAX came out of the US synthetic-fiber industry as producers learned to engineer fiber cross-sections for comfort, and it has become a common reference in sweat and comfort research. Since 2013 studies have used it as a benchmark wicking polyester in manikin, skin-wetness and ultraviolet-protection tests, and since 2020 as the wicking element in woven and stitched textile microfluidic devices for sweat sensing. It was attributed to INVISTA in 2013 and is now presented by The LYCRA Company, which emerged from Chapter 11 in May 2026. Launch dates and inventors could not be verified for this entry.
